en: The Pārājika of Mañjuśrī. Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels:
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the supreme and unsurpassed Triple Gem.
Having prostrated, Mañjuśrī, the mine of compassion, suddenly spoke. ||1||
All living beings are submerged in the most terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
O Protector, O Sage, show me how they shall deliver me. (2)
From the family of Ājīvika down to the very limit of the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), how could one of such pure lineage as a son be subject to a defeat (pārājika)? ||3||
The Blessed One said: "Listen now,
Mañjuśrī."
He whose sole great delight is the welfare of sentient beings;
for indeed, there are those born of the [four] castes: Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. ||4||
She was a Śūdra woman, devoid of the sacraments for the three higher castes;
she was virtuous, possessed of honor and beauty, and on the fourth day after her menses, she approached him.
The mutual affection between husband and wife is the cause for the seed to sprout;
when the fertile season has arrived, if there is no giver, I do not obtain the fruit.
By observing vows, restraints, and fasting for one month, she becomes pure;
then, when the time for conception arrives, the virtuous woman should perform the prescribed ritual procedure.
In the eighth month of the sixty-fourth [lunar cycle], the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) and other rites are performed;
this first consecration is for the embryos of all three types of women.
Having given birth to her child, he should undergo all the purificatory rites;
he should have the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and the others performed by nine or eleven Brahmins. ||9||
One should perform the consumption of honey and other rites as prescribed by the rules of ritual action;
furthermore, for the sake of satisfying the ancestors and the gods, one should cause the worship according to the injunctions to be performed.
Placing the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) foremost, one should cultivate the three concentrations. ||10||
Then, having performed the fire-oblation for the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should worship the Cow according to the prescribed ritual.
(1) The materials for the *arghya* offering are proclaimed to be: the fruit of the *kola*, unbroken grains, rice, barley, mustard seeds, honey, curd, milk, clarified butter, and water. ||11||
Having heard the nine-limbed teaching, one who possesses faith in the nine limbs is praised;
[he is like] a newborn human protected by the arrangement of the nine limbs. (12)
Then, preceded by the cultivation of emptiness, they should sever the navel;
for whatever is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata, that is the intrinsic nature of this world. (13)
The Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature, and this world is without intrinsic nature; he is wise, possesses the dhāraṇīs, is endowed with mindfulness, and is born with such speech. (14)
One should have him consume clarified butter while reciting the *paṭhastam* [mantra], preceded by the pronouncement of auspiciousness (*svastivācana*).
Likewise, one should perform the ritual bathing, the giving of gifts, and the celebration of auspicious festivities.
Once the severing of the umbilical cord has been performed, that period is designated as *sūtaka* (birth-impurity). ||15||
At the conclusion of the birth-impurity period, one should perform worship and cause auspicious rites to be carried out;
then, having bestowed the consecration, one should again offer blessings and so forth. ||16||
Thus concludes the procedure for the birth-rite and the cutting of the umbilical cord.
In that same manner, one should perform the worship consisting of the cultivation of all three samādhis;
one should offer five or six *prasthas* of *śāli* rice and kindle a lamp on the sixth day.
In that very manner, one should perform the worship and the departure by means of a vigil;
having duly honored the planets and the Mothers, as prescribed in the *Grahasādhana*.
In the tenth or twelfth year, or again in the twenty-second,
the naming ceremony (nāmakarma) should be performed, especially for the various social classes (varṇas).
A sage is a Brahmin because he causes delusion [of the senses] by his characteristics; a Kṣatriya is auspicious;
a householder is a Vaiśya; and a Śūdra is so called from the grinding of grain.
Or alternatively:

The wise have declared that *śarman* is for a Brāhmaṇa, *varman* for a Kṣatriya, and *gupta* for a Vaiśya; and for women, [names] should follow this sequence. (2) Furthermore, for women, the name should consist of long vowels and be endowed with auspiciousness.
In the third or fourth month, one should show the sun to the child.
The first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) should take place either in the eighth month or after a year;
having placed the Tāraṇī [mantra] before him, one should perform the study of the scriptures and other arts and crafts.
Whichever [finger] first touches it, by that first one the child’s karma lives on.
One should cause the tonsure ceremony and the piercing of the ears to be performed according to their respective order. ||8||
And likewise for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
[the initiation] should take place in the seventh year from conception, or up until the twelfth year.

One should cause the ritual of the vow-initiation (*vratopanayana*) to be performed within the Buddha’s teaching, having placed the community of elders (*saṃgha*) and the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) at the forefront. (10)
O Mahāmati, these should be performed according to the ritual procedure of the *karmasūtra*:
first, the triple refuge is to be granted, followed by the five [vows] beginning with that of the disciple;
and likewise the vow of the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), even without the shaving of the hair. (11)
For householders, after first pronouncing the name [of the deceased], the *triyāhika* rite should be performed according to the rules of their respective community. 12.
Abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the drinking of intoxicants—these five constitute the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*). (13)
Then, having shaved off the hair, one should leave a tuft on the head;
furthermore, the saffron robe should be given, and the ten precepts (śikṣāpada) should be administered again.
Dancing, singing, and instrumental music; garlands, perfumes, and ointments; the use of high beds, as well as high seats. (15)
Eating at improper times, gold, silver, and the ten things not to be accepted;
then the three robes, the alms-bowl, and the water-pot. (16)
One should cause him to receive the saṃghāṭī, the undergarment, and the kṣirīkā;
having attained the six perfections and the restraint of the Noble Truths and so forth. (17)
In their presence, he should cause them to receive the ten million precepts and the spirit of enlightenment.
These are the monks and novices who are to be gathered. (18)
And because of the cultivation of the three vehicles through that very [practice], the monk is foremost among all, being free from sacrificial rites and the like. (19)

Because it is the basis for nirvāṇa by virtue of its nature of non-dependence, the vajra, bell, and so forth, as well as the fire sacrifice (homa), are the means for accomplishing all activities. ||20||
Furthermore, the rank of Vajrācārya should be conferred by these two alone;
likewise, one should recite the mantras beginning with the *sūtra* and show the mandala.
The vessel [is purified] in the twelfth year, as are the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama);
for the three castes, [the purification occurs] in the fifth, eleventh, and sixteenth years respectively.
And the initiation ceremony (upanayana) should be performed as prescribed in the Deśatantra;
likewise, the cutting of the topknot (śikhāccheda) is for the monks and the disciples (śrāvakas). ||23||
Furthermore, he is the practitioner of the mantra of the yoga of renunciation, the wearer of the triple-braided hair,
and the one who possesses the patched robe, the monastic garment, the lower cloth, the realm of phenomena, and food.
The water-pot is the very sign, possessing the purity of the five knowledges;
likewise, the vajra is the means (upāya), while the ghaṭāṭhā is of the nature of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). ||25||
In both the conventional and ultimate truths, the Buddha is not created by the knowledge of suchness;
he stands at the forefront of all phonemes, possessing a radiance equal to twelve suns. ||26||
I bow to those who pervade the three worlds; may I always bow to them.
Thus ends the third chapter, the procedure for taking up the life of renunciation.
I pay homage to the offspring of the Śākya lineage, who is born through his very birth.
Having taken up the going-forth, the monk returns once more as a Vajradhṛk.
Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I shall proclaim the conduct of the world,
by which one constantly proceeds [toward the goal] that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(2) Having risen in the morning, the pure-souled one should again stand facing the east.
One should perform recitation and praise through the yoga of identifying oneself with one's own presiding deity. ||3||
Then, having performed the placement of the ten limbs, one should go outside.
One *kośa* or half of that [distance] outside the city, at a reservoir of water. ||4||
One should take earth for cleansing the teeth according to the distinction of social classes.
White, red, yellow, and black [flowers] should be offered upon pure grounds. ||5||
And likewise for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras as well.
At a river, a temple, a shrine, a cremation ground, or in malevolent locations; ||6||
In that case, clay should not be taken for specific rites on the path.
In cow-pens, in heaps of ashes, and in the pavilions of hermitages.
One should not exert effort in the rites concerning the paths of feces;
nor [should one use] the sacrificial tree, the cow’s milk-tree, the khadira, the amuṭa, or the arka.
And one should take Apāmārga and Kadamba for cleaning the teeth.
At that time, one should not pick up blades of grass or clods of earth with the eight fingers.
In the absence of tooth-sticks, where purity is achieved by means of mouthfuls of water, one should not toss the earth about; one should carry the robe on the head.
One should avoid facing the wind or urinating while facing it;
or alternatively:
Facing east at sunrise and facing north at midday. ||11||
They know that at the time of the two twilights and during the night, one should face south;
having covered the excrement and urine, one should then perform purification.
First is purification with water, second is purification with earth;
one should wash again constantly until no odor remains. (13)
One should wash the hands repeatedly according to the manner of drinking;
one should discharge three, five, or seven mouthfuls of water [for rinsing].
Such is the purification for householders, and it is especially so for those who wear rags.
For śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus, it should be double or triple [the size]. ||15||
One should always wash both hands and touch the tip of the mouth;
having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) by means of the "self-tirtha," one becomes eternally pure. ||16||
When one sips water (ācamana) with the tip of a fingernail, it is equal to drinking impurity;
likewise for one who has a head-wrap, loose hair, or a discarded upper garment, [and] together with... ||17||
Having sipped water, one should wash both hands and feet; by so sipping, one becomes pure.
Thus is the exposition on purity.
Now follows the procedure for bathing.
Meditation is the bath for monks, and the mantra for novices;
for those with rags as clothing it is bathing in water, and especially for Brahmins. ||1||
The body has nine apertures, is smeared with impurities, foul-smelling, soiled, and unclean; it is purified through meditation, therefore one should always perform ritual bathing.
First is the bath of purification from impurities; second is the bath of mantra;
third is the bath of meditation; and immediately after that is the offering of water. ||3||
As long as this libation does not cause pain to the inner garment, it is acceptable;
however, if one should cause pain through ignorance, his bath is fruitless.
Those fools who, during bathing and giving, always wash away their vision, have established [the deity] in a place other than the location previously intended. ||5||
He who, out of delusion, performs libations, bathing, giving gifts, sacrifice, meditation, and likewise the recitation of mantras on the Revā, which is free from all defects— [6]
All those various rites that have been performed go to waste;
therefore, having sipped water three times, one should touch the sense-base of the eyes.
One should perform the entire deposition of the deities (*nyāsa*), followed again by *prāṇāyāma* and the rest;

first the libation to the deities (*devatā-tarpaṇa*) and afterwards the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*). (8) [Then] the water-offering for the deceased (*preta-añjali*) should be performed, and thereafter one should wring out the garment and other items.
The going for the three refuges and also the confession of misdeeds. ||9||
One should always recite three times: rejoicing in [virtues] from the past, the undertaking of vows and so forth, and the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). ||10||
Then, having purified his soul and being devoted to mental vows, he should perform the worship of the Caitya, restraining his senses and remaining intent on pure conduct. (11)
Through the entry into the beginner's practice,
one should always perform all that ritual action as prescribed, including the daily worship.

One should perform the obligatory daily bath on the occasion of seeing Rāhu (an eclipse), after shaving, following a bad dream, after sexual intercourse, upon death, at a sacred ford, on special occasions, and on festival days.
The one of great intelligence who constantly practices according to this method attains the state of Buddhahood at the seat of enlightenment in this very life. (14)
If a monk eats his meal in the forenoon during seven auspicious ghaṭikās, or in the afternoon during seven [ghaṭikās], it is for all [monks] when the sun is situated [in its course]. 15.
One should not eat when the sun has set, except for food required by a vow or for a specific occasion; such a meal is as equal to the food of a ghost and becomes fruitless. (16)
One should never eat from trees that serve as components of a sacrifice;
even if one has eaten from such a tree through negligence, one should observe the poṣadha vow.
One should perform the sprinkling and the offering of food in triangular, circular, and square shapes, according to the distinctions of their respective classes and colors. (18)
Food and drink that are unwholesome, eating at night which is blameworthy, always consuming ghee after a meal, and likewise the eating of beef; ||19||
Then one should take the offering of bali and flowers, as well as the water for rinsing the mouth and the arghya;
thereafter, one should perform the fivefold purification (pañcapūtana), which brings delight to the inner self.
In this manner, the monk as well as the novice should feed [the guests];
having performed the protection with the mantra, he should feed them with a pure mind.
(21) And the Vajrācārya, along with the five [disciples] including the Grāhaka, should always eat the food.
The first vessel is the fire of nectar, which brings satisfaction; the second is the libation to the Mother Cows. ||22||
One-third [of the food] is for guests, while the fourth offering is for the *bali* spirits;
the remainder, however, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*) should feed for the sake of fully nourishing the five vital breaths (*vāyu*).
The ring finger is the prāṇa wind, the middle finger is indeed the apāna, the index finger is to be known as the samāna, and the little finger is the dāna wind. ||24||
The Vyāna wind is indeed the eldest, consisting of the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
the collection of the five fingers is the propitiation of the ten winds. (25)
One observing the vow should not eat with a cloth over the head, nor likewise while standing on the feet; one should also avoid sitting in the *utkuṭaka* posture and laughing during the meal. (26)

One should avoid what has been tasted by a dog, what has been licked, what has been roared over, what has a deformed face, and that which has been vomited from the mouth after being drunk and then partially swallowed again. (27)
Be vigilant; having become one whose impurities are dried up day by day, you shall be purified through meditation and recitation. ||28||
The ancestors and deities are satisfied by the pressure of the water spat out from the mouthful;
therefore, one's leavings should be given, for the remaining food is that which gratifies the spirits (bhūtas). 29.
Afterwards, one should rinse the mouth with the remainder of what was set aside;
then, one should perform the purification that consists in the emptiness of contact with impurity. (30)
Thereafter, one should recite the sūtras and listen to the compendium of the Dharma;
subsequently, at the time of twilight, one should again practice the meditation on the mantra. (31)
Having ascended at the time of twilight and focused his mind on the meditation of the Guru,
he first prostrated before the divine Guru and performed the recitation and hymn with a concentrated mind.
In the north he placed his head, and in the west,
the wise one himself ascended the lion-bed, intent upon the meditative concentration of the dhāraṇī.
Thus ends the *Nityācāravidhi* spoken by the venerable Lord Muni-Indra, Bhagavān Māghana.
(8) Then Mañjuśrī addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Sage, I have heard the nectar issued from the mouth of the glorious one. (1)
If some should, through negligence, violate their vows, observances, and daily duties, how should one confess their *pārājika* offenses? Please explain this, O Tathāgata. (2)
The Blessed One said:
"One should not, through negligence, transgress one's duty, nor one's vows and observances;
by means of giving, dharma, and fasting for a month, one is released from sin. (3)
One who has fallen away from the worship of daily rites, as well as from recitation and meditation,
shall become pure by means of bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and a three-night vigil.
When one has fallen away due to lust, anger, and the like, and is being cooked in the Raurava hell, one is purified by means of bathing, giving gifts, and fasting for the duration of one year. ||5||
Whatever sin is committed by speech is proclaimed as a *pātaka*; whatever action is committed by the body becomes a *mahāpārājika*. (6)
Whatever sin is committed through the mind is called a minor offense (upapātaka);
there are four verbal sins and three types of bodily sins.
Furthermore, these three born of the mind are the roots of evil: taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct—these constitute bodily [evil]. (8)
Whatever evil has been committed with the body is liberated through bodily austerity; likewise, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and divisive talk [are abandoned]. (9)
Even verbal evil committed is released through bodily austerity;
as are ignorance, malice, and wrong view born of the mind. (10)
Whatever sin has been committed with the mind is liberated through mental penances;
even that which is impure becomes entirely purified by the consumption of mantras.
Water held in the hand becomes pure by contact with the sun or fire, or by placing it on the ground.

[Impurity occurs] from seeing or touching that which is undesirable, or from touching what has been used for eating or is leftover; likewise from the discharge of feces or urine, and from seeing or touching that which is defiled. (12) (9)
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the touching [of the body] three, five, or seven times.
One should not incur any fault regarding touch; indeed, bathing shall bring purification in the case of a sacrifice, a wedding, a journey, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and in temples. 14.

During a regional upheaval or in battle, at a great feast or a social gathering, upon intentionally touching a corpse, or when encountering a woman who has recently given birth or is menstruating; (15)
A Cāṇḍāla, a cock, a fanged creature, one who commits great sins, one who sells meat or liquor, and furthermore, an attendant of the dead; ||16||
By performing a bath with one's clothes on and using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one becomes pure;
all contact resulting from negligence is purified by a mere bath alone. ||17||
During an eclipse, at a sacrifice, during the ritual bathing of deities at a sacred ford,
and when mounting a chariot according to local custom, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.

For a woman who has given birth, the ritual for the monthly period is completed after three nights; for a woman in childbirth, it is after ten days; and for a menstruating woman, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on after twelve days.
One should discard one's former garment and put on a pure garment after a bad dream, contact with an impure person, marriage, shaving, or sexual intercourse.
Bathing alone is prescribed when there is indigestion or during the period of ritual impurity (vṛddhi-kārya).
A husband and wife are always impure [after sexual union], but the man alone is impure on the bed. ||21||
A virtuous woman, having risen from her bed, is always pure;
just as gold becomes pure through burning, cutting, or rubbing. 22.

Rice, vegetables, roots, and fruits are purified by water from a conch shell; wood and earthenware are purified by washing and heating; [other] impure things are purified by cleansing and exposure to heat.
When touched by a Cāṇḍāla or others, an earthen vessel becomes pure when it is made of wood; however, one should avoid a vessel that has been used for excrement. ||25||
An object defiled by an impure touch becomes pure through the touch of earth;
all phenomena are pure by their very nature and are purified by that very nature.
(26) When an occasional rite has been performed during rites such as the offering of oblations to the *lakṣya*, [it is purified].
Then, O Blessed One, O Sage, how indeed does death occur within one's lineage and so forth? (26)
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, and I shall speak."
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, act even through other means; in that case, no fault is found. ||28||

If the death of someone belonging to the same lineage (gotra) occurs after one has performed the obligatory rites (naimittika), there is no fault whatsoever in performing sacrificial acts and other such duties for that person. 29.
As long as it has not reached the fourth day, one does not incur the state of impurity (sūtaka);
at its conclusion, however, one should perform whatever rites for impurity are prescribed.
In this regard, the method of purification is set forth through the prescribed rules for the proper performance of the rites concerning the bones,
for the sake of the liberation of embodied beings who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. (31)
As it has been said: "In the Sūtra, the purification of all refuges is taught for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, especially for those who are devoid of virtuous action. (32)
What is the use of a boat for those who possess the power to cross by themselves? For those who lack the power to cross on their own, that boat is of great importance. (34)
Through the nature of desire and by means of the state of perceiving phonemes,
one should again show the various characteristics of immortality to living beings.
Yellowish-green, white, yellow, and blue as the fifth;
through the purification of the five Buddhas, one should conceive of the five gnoses. ||35||

One should apply the movement of that very [reality] by means of its characteristic form, because the movement of mendicants, ascetics, Brahmins, and others is seen to be in accordance with reality. (36)
One should unite [the practitioner] with that which is pure and purified through the yoga of the process of withdrawal;
those who have not received initiation and are devoid of the application of mantra. ||37||
Having purified their miserable states, he shall establish them in Sukhāvatī.
May all beings—those born in water, those born on land, birds, and so forth—be purified of their miserable states and always established in perfect enlightenment. (38) (11)
The triple concentration, when practiced while seated, purifies committed sin. ||39||
One should arrange the mandala for the rite and apply the fivefold knowledge;
having worshipped the fire of dissolution with bitter wood such as that of the *nimba* tree.
One should propitiate the fire of dissolution with blue-colored offerings;
then one should carry [the remains] out from the village to a sacred bathing place or to a cremation ground. 41.
Whether it be a new lay devotee, a son, or even a disciple, one should always purify the miserable rebirths with streams of water from a water-pot. 42.
The formal conclusion of the vow should be performed, as well as the offering of funeral cakes and the water-rites;
likewise, the consecration of the first ground and the second [ground] with water. (43)
The third is the refinement of the vital energy (tejas), and the fourth is the mounting of the breath (prāṇa).
As long as the wind blows through the forest, so long does the path of birth exist. ||44||

The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed by one whose mind is focused on the spirits, until the remaining fires have been satiated, without allowing the body to come into contact with anything else. 45.
For that very [deity], the fire-mouth (agnimukha) should be performed according to its nature of being devoid of intrinsic selfhood (niḥsvabhāva).
The teacher and the disciple should be of the same lineage (sagotra) and of their own respective castes (svavarṇa), whether they be equal or unequal.
One should cause water to be offered for a deceased friend, son-in-law, or brother-in-law;
[the rite for] a child who has not yet cut teeth lasts until the completion of the fourth year.
A gift given to a carnivore does not make one pure after three nights;
when a child dies at birth, the father and mother remain impure for three nights. 48.
For the [remnants of] lineages, there is merely bathing; for the remainder, according to the division of years, when one who has gone forth but has not performed the initiation dies. ||49||
One should cause the offering of funeral cakes and the gift of water to be performed without hesitation;
likewise, one should honor the Vajrācārya, who is like the sky in color and possesses the immediate purity of space. 50.
A single funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered without distinction throughout the seven days.
When the third day arrives, the collection of bones and remains must be performed.
Then, having reduced those [remains] to ashes once more, one should have the remaining ashes carried away.
Starting from the third day, for five and seven days respectively. ||52||
And for the sake of purifying the miserable states of existence, one should gradually construct a maṇḍala;
one should place the bones in a river,
especially within the interior of a caitya.
One should cause the Amṛtodbhava Sūtra to be recited again and again;
when the seventh day arrives, one should have the purification rites performed.
One should provide bathing, shaving, clothing, and food for the Saṅgha;
thereafter, a single *piṇḍa* for the sake of enlightenment should be offered. (55)
One should likewise cultivate the cymbals (tāla) in accordance with the stability [of the mind].
Oṃ mune mune mahāmune svāhā. ||56||
Oṃ, homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the King who Purifies All Evil Destinies.
It is as follows: Oṃ śodhaya śodhaya viśodhaya viśodhaya sarvapāpopaśodhane | śuddhe viśuddhe sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhane svāhā ||57||
From this day forward, O Bhikṣu [Name], just as those Tathāgatas [dedicated themselves] to unexcelled perfect enlightenment, so do I dedicate for you. (58)
This procedure is prescribed for novice monks and bhikṣus; for lay followers who wear robes, however, the ritual action is distinct and the performance is separate. (59)
The purification consisting of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites is performed according to the distinctions of the four castes,
beginning from the first day up until the seventh day.
The offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be performed as required by one who is pure in soul and has conquered his senses;
he should cause one ball to be offered in each of the first, second, and third [sections].

In the same way, one should cause three [drops] to fall in either the fourth or the fifth [moment], for the sake of purifying the seven states of existence and cutting off all miserable rebirths. //62//
On the fifth day, the seven elements of the factors of enlightenment arise;
likewise, on the sixth day, one mass [is formed], and on the seventh day, two masses.
One should cause the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* to enter into meritorious activity.
And again, there is one auspicious nectar, the seed of enlightenment. ||64||
One should transform the mass [of food] and cast it into the presence of the Jina;
one should cause the dissolved mass to be offered, merged into the seven Tathāgatas. (65)
Furthermore, by way of conventional truth, there may be the marriage of cows and so forth.
Alternatively, one should contemplate the placement according to the process of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) by means of the seed-syllable of the mantra. ||66||
Due to the absence [of the father] and because it pertains to the monthly rite, the fourteenth pinda is offered again;
first the father, and then five more along with the vikara.
One should properly perform the *yoni* ceremony, just as one does for the father and mother.
The father [is the representative] of the grandfather and others, just as the mother [is for] the maternal grandmother.
One should apply the verse, "As our father and mother have gone," to the *alīna* [offering]. This is called the tenth *piṇḍa*, and it is for the deceased among all castes. (70)
A Kṣatriya becomes pure after ten days plus one.
For Vaiśyas it is twelve days, and for a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is one day.
This same purification is prescribed for both death and birth;
however, when one of a different caste has died, one remains impure for three nights after the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
At a sacrifice, a marriage, a religious rite, or at the moment of renunciation, one becomes pure instantly.
Mañjuśrī said this to the Blessed One: ||73||
If the father of one is living while the son has died, how can there be absorption into that [deity] during his funeral rite (śrāddha) when the ritual procedure is suspended? //74//
The Blessed One said:
"His father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—his refuge is the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; that is his destination. (75)
By this method, [the state] of all those whose karma has become latent is to be known. //76//

Now, concerning the *śrāddha* rice-ball (*piṇḍa*): (14) Beginning from the day following the *līna*, it is always recommended that the *śrāddha* rice-ball be offered at home for regular rites, as well as on special occasions, at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and in temples. 77.
One of perfectly composed mind should place all the substances—consisting of various kinds of food and drink, excluding anything contemptible—complete, stainless, and pure. (78)
On the previous day, one should invite the teacher and others for the purpose of a meal;
having washed one's own feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then touch them. 79.
Having respectfully seated the Guru on a seat in a pure place, one should offer him water for his feet and water for sipping, and then engage him in the rite at the site of the Śrāddha. 80.
If the Guru recites the mantra at the place where water for the feet and water for sipping should be placed during a Rākṣasa-śrāddha, all ritual actions shall become fruitless. (81)
Self-restrained, with a secret and pure self, having conquered the senses, observing silence, firm in his vows, free from desire, equally contented in all actions, pure, and patient; ||82||
One should, with a concentrated mind, install that very [image] during the *guru-śrāddha*;
thus the *śrāddha* becomes pure and reaches the ancestors as inexhaustible. (83)
One who is evil-minded, harsh in speech, mocking, fond of quarreling, discontented, fallen from purity—he indeed is devoid of a teacher. ||84||
The ancestors depart disappointed when the donor goes to hell;
one should avoid an iron vessel, a corpse-like vessel, and a wooden vessel for the śrāddha rite. 85.
Where a gift is given through negligence, it results in sin once bestowed; therefore, placing the realm of Dharma before one, one should provide fodder for cows. ||86||
Having lit a lamp, the wise person should worship with very smooth [incense];
likewise, according to the eighth-day vow, one should avoid [unpleasant] colors and fragrances.
Likewise, the wise man should avoid substances with scent during the śrāddha rite;
however, upon seeing incense made of jasmine flowers consecrated with mantras, the deities are gratified. (88)
If the father is satisfied, one should not go [to him], nor likewise if he is terrifying;
one should not offer scents and flowers at first, but should cause them all to be given afterwards.
The *nivāra* grass and flower, when joined with the mantra, are of great significance.
That alone is called a true *śrāddha*, for by it the ancestors are always satisfied. ||90||
In the absence of all [other materials], *kuśa* grass is best; in the absence of *kuśa*, there is the act of removal (*vyapakriyā*).
For all ritual purposes, *kuśa* is best, especially in sacrifices and ancestral rites (*śrāddha*). (91)
One should not have it made too long, nor too short, nor deficient in its womb;
one should cause it to be taken from pure ground with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths.

The eternal [mantra] is on the tip of the *kuśa* grass, likewise the immeasurable on the middle of the *kuśa*, and the agitating [mantra], which is the praise of the mantra, is on the root of the *kuśa*. 93.
A person who gives these—nirvāṇa, a monk, a novice, and a mendicant’s robe—is rare; by giving them, one attains imperishability. 94.
These are the vessels that must always be used in the rites of *śrāddha* in the absence of kinsmen such as those of the same lineage (*sagotra*), or in the absence of one's own son. (95)
If one is on a journey, living with a son, or in a foreign land during a time of upheaval;
or if there is a lack of food, or when the recipient is a worthy person, yet the wife is in her menses; ||96||
When a wife residing in a foreign land dies, if her husband constantly offers a ball of raw rice (āmapiṇḍa), it shall attain imperishability even after being given. ||97||
With roots, fruits, vegetables, flowers, or even grass, one of pure soul performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) with devotion. (98)
When that virtuous woman is in her menses, she alone shall remain pure;
by merely bathing, the husband shall become pure for all ritual acts. (99)
If, once the day has been ascertained, anyone should cause the Śrāddha to be ruined, the ancestors depart in despair and the destruction of the lineage occurs. (100)
If death, menstruation, or birth-impurity occurs during the interval of a *śrāddha*, those [impurities] and that [interruption] render the rite fruitless;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should give the offering at a time free from such obstacles. 101.
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on each day up to the full moon,
one should offer the *dharmapiṇḍa* for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life.
[102] (16) [This should be done] in Kārttika, Mādhava, Māgha, and Śrāvaṇa, at the conclusion of the Yugas.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, and on the third lunar day of the month presided over by Mādhava (Vaiśākha).

Likewise, on the full moon day of Māgha, or on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa—by whomsoever a funeral cake (piṇḍa) is offered there, it shall yield immeasurable fruit. (104)
First, one should wash the feet; afterwards, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one should sprinkle water over oneself.
Then, the observer of the vow should perform the six-limbed recitation and meditate upon selflessness (nairātmya). 105.
When one proceeds toward the half [of the path] while facing the east, having taken dūrvā sprouts, kuśa grass, water, and clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds. (106)
Facing south, he should likewise place the preceptor facing east,
and the noble Saṃgha facing north, upon pure grounds.
With a mind full of devotion, one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, food, and the formal ritual intention (saṃkalpa) to the Guru and the noble Saṅgha. 108.
One should offer the *godhana* for those in the miserable realms and provide the *piṇḍa* for the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
During a *śrāddha* performed with graceful gestures, one should worship the *dharmastūpa*.
One should always worship with the offering of a *piṇḍa*, not by mere discarding;
having sipped water (*ācamana*), one should always employ all the fingers with the palm facing upwards.
All holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, enter into the palms of one's hands;
therefore, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at a true holy ford and avoid the remaining ones. 111.
The kusha grass seat, the vessel for liquor, and likewise the seat for the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should first be placed before the father; afterwards, one should cause the rice-balls to be offered.
Without a modification, the mass would suffer the pain of a million masses;
therefore, one should cause a modification to be applied to all within the self. (113)
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor,
the dismissal of the ritual cakes (piṇḍavisarjana) follows;
then the preceptor should likewise perform the bestowing of blessings and the consecration (abhisevana).
Having placed the vessel containing the piṇḍas on the ground outside the altar,
and having circumambulated it while pouring streams of water, he should bow facing westward;
thereafter, he should distribute [the portions] to the ancestors with this verse.
And at the abode of the pretas, at sacred fords, at ponds, lakes, and lotus-pools. ||116||

Constantly offering the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and perpetually performing the śrāddha for the deceased, you have acted for the sake of all sentient beings; having attained accomplishment, proceed according to your followers. (117)
Go to the domain of the Buddha and return once more; just as knowledge is transmitted from preceptor to pupil, or as one lamp is lit from another. (118)
And another mudrā of the mudrā is the face reflected from the face in a mirror;
one should eat the remainder of the rice-ball and the food together with one's kinsmen. ||119||
At midday, or at night, or at the end of the day during the three watches—these are all times for the rice-ball offering; however, one should avoid doing so during the night.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa).
Due to negligence, by being struck by a weapon, or through suicide and untimely death;
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should cause their *piṇḍa* offering to be given. ||1||
The Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten days, the Kṣatriyas after twelve days, the Vaiśya after fifteen days, and the Śūdra becomes pure after a month. ||2||

If the sun rises while the night has already begun, that day is to be taken as the first; likewise, when death occurs during the menstrual flow or the period of birth-impurity, the day is to be reckoned from the start.

One who suffers a miscarriage should cause women to recite [the mantra] over it; and she in whose month the fetus is situated likewise incurs the impurity (sūtaka). As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, so long one does not incur the impurity of birth.
Thereafter, once the stalk has been severed, the birth-impurity (sūtaka) is prescribed.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a wedding, in a sacrificial circle,
in a monastic community, in a hermitage, or on a riverbank, one should not observe ritual impurity (sūtaka) at those times.

One should prescribe immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) in the case of water containing a waterfall or fire, or from falling from a tree in the forest, as well as upon renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). ||7|| (18)

One should remain pure during the tonsure ceremony for ordination, at weddings, festivals, and sacrifices; likewise, one remains pure at the commencement of a *śrāddha*, a rite of passage (*vṛddhi*), or a festival, even when there is birth or death impurity (*mṛtasūtake*).
Upon hearing that a kinsman has died in another country, the relatives must observe immediate purification;
likewise, for those of the same lineage (sagotra), there is a ten-day period of impurity for the mother and father.
Upon the death of a paternal uncle, a sister’s son, their sons, or a daughter’s son, as well as upon the death of one’s father or mother, one shall remain pure after three nights.
In the case of a death, a hired laborer, and a woman who has given birth, as well as the woman herself, she shall be pure at that very moment, provided it does not happen otherwise. ||11||
One who has become impure through a death is not purified by a birth of a child or by a birth of a cow;
a heavy impurity is purified by a light one, but a light impurity does not purify a heavy one. ||12||
And for one who has emerged from the womb but is a child who has not yet cut his teeth, one should not perform the water-libations nor the purificatory rites for them. (13)
If a child dies before its teeth have erupted, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed;
if the child has already erupted teeth, the father and brother shall become pure after three nights. ||14||
When a father, mother, or preceptor passes away, one should designate the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) until the shaving ceremony has been performed. 15.
If someone dies in another country and the day is unknown,
one should adopt the day when it becomes known and perform the ritual offerings of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for purification.
One who is engaged in the offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for a preta should perform a bath with his clothes on;
by the mere act of bathing, or through the recitation of mantras, the practitioner of mantra becomes pure. ||17||
When the tenth day has arrived, one should not have a haircut;
indeed, at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or on ground outside the village, one's garment should be discarded there.
If one's father, who is a great guru, should ever meet with misfortune,
one should perform bathing, giving of gifts, worship, and other rites for one year.
For six months for one's mother, for the same duration for one's wife, and for that same duration for one's brothers and sons—in some cases, purification is produced.
(20) (19) Mañjuśrī said this to the Blessed One: "No."
How indeed is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense a "Great *Pārājika*" again?
How can there be liberation for one who has committed a *pārājika*? Please explain this, O Great Sage! (21)
The Blessed One said:
"For those who have killed an Arhat, the penance shall last twenty-four years;
and for a renunciant who has committed the murder of a Brahmin, one should perform it for twelve years. (22)

Having observed the poṣadha vows daily, and furthermore performing worship at the caityas, one who has conquered the senses should constantly practice bathing, giving, recitation, and meditation. (23)
By giving a gift according to one's means—such as gold, a communal meal for the Saṅgha, or the gift of a hundred cows—one is liberated from sins with great difficulty. (24)
One who kills an ascetic, as well as one who kills a Brāhmaṇa woman,
shall perform that very same vow for sixteen years or half of that time.
One who kills a śramaṇa, as well as a śrāmaṇera, and one who kills a celaka, shall observe [the vow] for ten years. ||26||
One who has killed a Kṣatriya shall likewise perform this for ten years;
as before, he should observe the Saptamī vow, the Kaṭhinī rite, ritual bathing, and the giving of gifts. (27)
Anyone who kills a Vaiśya shall perform [the penance] for eight years;
the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall likewise perform the aforementioned rites of bathing and giving gifts.
One who has conquered his senses and is a slayer of a Kṣatriya woman should perform the pure gift of one hundred and one bulls for one year in that very place. ||28||
Anyone who kills a Vaiśya shall perform the penance for eight years;
for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa, the aforementioned rites of bathing and giving gifts must be performed.
Upon the occurrence of the killing of a Vaiśya woman, one who has conquered the senses shall practice celibacy for six years,
performing acts such as giving gifts as previously prescribed.
One who kills a Śūdra shall perform the vow for six years,
diligently observing the prescribed fasts and restraints as before.
One who kills a Śūdra woman shall likewise perform it for five years.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, meditation, as well as the kṛcchra penance and the upoṣadha fast; ||32||
Thus ends the section on the *pārājika* offense regarding the killing of those belonging to the four castes and so forth.
And for killing a cow, one who has subdued the senses shall perform the twelve-year penance while staying in a cow-pen.
The gift of cows, the gift of land, and especially the observance of the Poṣadha; ||1||
Devotion to cows, feeding a hundred cows, the dedication of a stūpa and so forth, and the constant consumption of cow dung—one should perform these as part of the Kṛcchra penance during the vow. (2)
In the case of killing a pregnant woman, the fine is double;
for killing a horse, ten *adhas* [of gold]; and likewise for killing an elephant, eight.
In the case of striking another, the penance lasts six years; for killing a pregnant woman, it is double that amount;
and likewise for striking with a staff, using weapons, or causing falls and drowning in water.
If, through negligence, he does not go [to the temple] for five or seven days, he should perform half of that penance for each day of neglect.
If he does not go due to negligence, he should perform that [penance] for up to seven days.
To that extent they are not defiled, and at its conclusion they become purified;
this occurs through the offering of medicinal herbs, whether by one's own will or by the power of a restraint.
There is no fault in that death; no injury to living beings is incurred.
One should accept food and drink; however, if one drinks, one should drink only water.
In cases of loss, theft, or such [damage], no compensation for the destruction of life is obtained.
A man may face death when engaged in the pursuit of wealth, in travel, or even in illness. ||8||
One should die right there; one incurs no guilt for the killing of a pregnant woman, nor for a single quarter [of the sin] in cases of disease, capture, or confinement. (9)
And one should also observe the vow for a distance of three-quarters of a yojana;
that practice is praised for one who has committed a sin intentionally. ||10||
For those who have committed sins unintentionally, there is merely the purification of the body;
likewise, there is the binding of the hair, shaving, and the diligent discarding of clothes. (11) Furthermore, there is the gift of cows and gold, as well as the feeding of the Saṅgha.
By this, one is released from sin committed unintentionally.
Even a sin committed intentionally is liberated through the *kṛcchra* penance,
[as well as sins related to] nourishing, feeding, affection, [the act of] *gharāṭhā*, supporting, and adorning.
Whether one is submerged in a mire of floodwaters, struck by a thunderbolt, fallen among beasts of prey, or in a forest fire; ||14||
If an obstacle should arise therein, one should perform one quarter [of the practice]. ||15||
A Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or likewise a Śūdra woman should observe the vow in the same manner;
or, if death should occur through negligence when the pregnancy is complete. ||16||
Through the performance of half of that vow, purification of the body arises;
[otherwise] the killing of a father or the killing of a Brahmin would be equal to a pārājika offense. (17)
If the killing of a mother should occur through negligence—whether it be equal to the killing of a cow—or if it is committed out of anger, with intentional desire, or by one's own will; ||18||
Whether in this world or the next, impurity is like an adamantine coating;
even if one has a son, it would be equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Furthermore, through his deliberation, he seeks humiliation by means of seizing fields, houses, gold, cattle, and women. (20)
In such a time of evil action, oppressed by the wind and heat, [one may act] for one's own sake, for the sake of one's father and mother, and likewise for the sake of teachers and kinsmen. (21)
He for whose sake one might give up one's life would himself be the sinner;
this applies especially to children, the elderly, women, and the sick. (22)
Or even for one who has performed a sacrifice with a desire for merit, half a share should be given as long as the boy is being celebrated [as such] until his twelfth year. ||23||
Until he reaches eighty years of age and becomes an aged and wretched man, he should diminish his portion by one through giving and take for himself only one share of the subjects' wealth. (22) (24)
One should perform one-third of that [penance] by which one is liberated from those sins;
for the killing of all outcastes (antyaja) and others, one should perform the Kṛcchra-Ṣoḍaśaka penance. ||25||
With a concentrated mind, he shall perform the vow for three years, along with giving gifts, recitation, and ritual bathing. ||26||
Thus ends the section on the determination [of the time].
He who, out of a desire for innocent fish and other aquatic creatures, enters the water where the *khecarī* dwells, is himself a slayer of living beings. (1)
The killing of a serpent is equal to the killing of a Brahmin, and the killing of a deer is the same as [the killing of] a Vaiśya.
In the same way, one incurs the sin of violence by killing a lion or a member of the kṣatriya caste. ||2||
The Śukrasāraka, Kauśca, and others, as well as the peacock and other birds that move through the sky;
In cases of hatred, one should be known as having committed a *pārājika* offense; purification occurs after three nights. ||3||
Sparrows, cuckoos, and bees were brought down by intoxication and greed.
One becomes pure in a single day through bathing, giving gifts, and fasting. ||4||
The cranes, lapwings, swans, ruddy geese, and those dwelling in the *akula* trees;
the deer, lions, elephants, horses, and even all the monkeys. (5)
Cats, pigs, snakes, terrifying creatures, and likewise fish.
Through delusion or through a fall [into a lower realm], one becomes pure after three nights. ||6||
One should give gifts to the Brahmins and feed the noble Saṅgha;
one should mutter the mantra mentally and recite the hymn of praise aloud.
Thus concludes the offense of expulsion for killing.
Having attained the state of Buddhahood, what else would he perform?
For from that state of individuality, one shall again attain Buddhahood. ||1||

One who has attained each individual stage should practice among the Śrāvakas; one should always practice among the Śrāvakas and not, however, among the Pratyekabuddhas. (2) (23) In the same way, one should practice toward Brāhmaṇas and others within the class of Kṣatriyas.
When one has sons and grandsons, then one should feed [the guests] at that very time. ||3||
In the same way, a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra should act accordingly;
when a son or grandson is born from one's own caste, he should be known as fallen. ||4||
In this way, others are to be known as belonging to the family when they are cast into a different family; until the fetus is born, it does not even arise from the pregnant woman's own family. ||5||
Purification must be performed for that long; no other purity is obtained.
This concludes the section on those who have fallen (patita) and those who have committed the pārājika offenses. 6.
For monks who eat at improper times, there is an offense when seven ghaṭikās have elapsed.
By means of a single day of vows and fasting, one shall become pure. ||7||
And one should perform [the rite] by eating [the substance], provided it is other than the noble restriction.
And even for eating what is unfit to be eaten, one becomes pure after six years. ||8||

In the same way, if one eats from anyone other than those of one's own caste—whether from Brahmins and so forth, or even from one who has fallen from his own caste—one shall remain pure after one year. ||9||
Also upon touching another's wife, or stepping over the shadow of a sacred shrine (caitya) and so forth.
In approaching a woman of low birth, one is purified in three months. ||10||
Whether by the fault of association with affection, or by punishment, or even by force.
When he eats food from one of low caste, he becomes pure after one month. ||11||
If one follows the customs of a family other than one's own caste, or eats food that is forbidden to eat,
or drinks water from one of a lower caste, one becomes pure after half a month.
Upon taking possession of a woman who has a "field-disease" (kṣetriṇī), a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights;
likewise when taking possession of one from among Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth. ||13||
Even from one's own family, there is the taking of those who are of low caste or of one's own inferior birth.
A pure man becomes purified by means of the distinction of qualities after seven nights. ||14||
When one eats with prior knowledge [of the impurity], purification does not exist again. ||15||
One should overcome those of inferior caste on that day during a conflict of anger;
thereafter, having observed the ritual at the throat for three nights, one becomes pure. (16)
One becomes pure in seven nights after a conflict involving the pulling of hair;
there is no fault in the act of applying oil for the purpose of removing hair with a razor.

In cases of birth-impurity or death-impurity, as well as when one has eaten excessively out of negligence, one becomes pure through intense vows and fasting, bathing, and the use of cow-products (gavya). 18.
If monks eat at the house of a cairaka, as does a novice monk,
they become pure after five nights, even if it be during a death-impurity or a birth-impurity. ||19||
In this manner, a Brāhmaṇa and others shall become pure after three nights.
Thus concludes the instruction on what is fit to be eaten, what is not to be eaten, and purity.
When the vessels of liquor, spirits, and wine remain, and when milk and water remain well-settled.
Where one drinks [liquor] through negligence, one becomes pure after three nights.
If one drinks water that has been partially consumed by another, one should abandon the resulting knowledge [of the rite];
one becomes pure in a single day by means of bathing, fasting, and the products of the cow (gavya). ||2||
If someone should, through negligence, eat ten onions, he becomes purified by fasting for seven nights. ||3||
If a disciple eats meat from aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial creatures,
he becomes pure after seven nights by means of bathing, fasting, and the products of the cow. ||4||
There is no purity for one who drinks liquor, especially for monks;
therefore, one should avoid drinking liquor, whether out of negligence or delusion. (5)
If a child possessed by a spirit dies, one should not find fault in that matter;
if the child should live through a month-long fast as part of a vow, then he becomes pure.
Whatever sin has been committed, whether preceded by a sense of gratitude or otherwise;
For them there is neither purity nor sin, especially for those who possess knowledge. ||7||
For a novice monk, a wandering mendicant, and a lay follower, one shall be pure by the end of the day, regardless of whether the place is accessible or inaccessible. ||8||
If a Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra unintentionally approaches one who is forbidden as a sexual partner by another of these classes, he is purified through the performance of a penance. (25) 9.
Likewise, the wives of teachers, as well as one's mother, mother-in-law, maternal aunt, female friend, paternal aunt, wife of a maternal uncle, the wife of a disciple, and sisters; ||10||
The ascetic daughter, kinsmen who have sought refuge, one abandoned by her nurse, a Kshatriya, the best of the three castes, and a devoted wife. ||11||

If one should go there for the very purpose of returning, he alone becomes a violator of the Guru's bed; the great sin of violating the Guru's bed is as indelible as adamantine cement for those who dwell there.
By performing vows, penances, and fasts, or even by the sacrifice of one's life,
one is liberated from the most terrible sin of violating the Guru’s bed, which is as firm as an adamantine coating.
A sinner is liberated from sin through the destruction of the body upon going to a sacred ford (sutīrtha);
likewise, women go back and forth [to such places] out of delusion.

One is liberated from [the sin of] violating the guru’s bed by observing vows, fasting, and visiting sacred sites; this is the instruction. It is accomplished through the musical instrument of meditation when the noble Saṃgha has entered into cessation.
A bhikṣu is purified in one day; a śrāmaṇeraka in three nights. ||16||
A *celaka* shall become pure after six days in the event of birth or death impurity;
a *bhikṣu* is purified after seven days, and a *śrāmaṇeraka* after half a fortnight. (17)
A water-pot becomes pure by being rinsed twenty-one times during the impurity caused by birth or death;
likewise, there is but a single funeral ball (piṇḍa) for those under vows and for mendicants as well.
One should cause the ten funeral rice-balls (daśapiṇḍa) to be offered for the Cera, the Upāsakas, and the others;
indeed, all of them must receive the ten rice-balls individually and separately to ensure their purification. (19)
For the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, purification shall occur respectively after ten days, twelve days, one fortnight, and one month. (20)
The rite of shaving is prescribed for those of the same lineage (sagotra), as well as for one's father and kinsmen;
one becomes pure by bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). ||21||
One becomes pure after three nights in the prescribed order for the maternal relatives, as well as for a sister’s son, a sister’s husband, a daughter, and a daughter’s husband. (26) [Verse 22]
In the case of a father-in-law, a brother-in-law’s son, a friend, a fellow student, or a kinsman, one becomes pure after three nights; for others, by mere bathing. ||23||
The rites should be performed by a son who offers the funeral ball (piṇḍa), or by a wife, or by a brother;
and in the absence of a son, they must be performed by kinsmen of the same lineage (sagotra) and others. ||24||
One should take great care not to neglect the mantra of samādhi;
even during periods of impurity or death, one should avoid worldly customs.
One should not perform bathing, giving gifts, fasting, Vedic study, vows, or auspicious rites when the period of impurity for the deceased or for birth has occurred. //26//
When impurity due to birth or death has occurred, one should not perform acts of giving;
nor should one undertake the instruction of vows, Vedic study, or marriage. ||27||
Thus is the exposition on purity.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which consists of the vows and the pārājika rules—the liberation from all sins and the destruction of all afflictions. (1)
Starting from the first day, one should observe the eightfold fast;
having reached the second day, one should prescribe the hearing of the Dharma.
On the third day, one should undertake the recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, and so forth;
on the fourth day, one should engage in the meditation upon and service of the Guru. ||3||
On the first day, one should perform the *poṣadha*; on the second day, the *ayācita* (unasked) vow; and on the third day, one should indeed observe the *nakṣatra-darśana* (the lunar mansion). ||4||
On the fourth day, one should indeed observe the fast by abstaining from food;
one should perform all rites such as bathing and giving gifts, and partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). ||5||
On the fifth day, one should cause [the ritual] to be performed and feed the noble Saṃgha;
afterwards, one should indeed break the fast, and at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast, one should become pure. ||6||
Pure in soul and having conquered his senses, he constantly observed his vow.
Thus ends the instruction on the vows.
(27) Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter as the seventh, and water from a sacred bathing place combined together are known as *pañcagavya*. 1.
A Brāhmaṇa should likewise drink the three products of the cow;
a Kṣatriya should wear them on his head, and a Vaiśya should indeed apply them to his eyes.
Indeed, for women and Śūdras, as well as for others, this is very difficult to obtain even by looking at it.
Especially for the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. ||3||
One should eat the fruit of the two-fold cooking [only] when it is free from the customs of one's own family;
otherwise, just as a monk’s drinking of liquor leads to falling into hell, so too would it be for him. ||4||
Cow’s urine is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in the *devayajña*; then cow dung is the splendor of Varuṇa;
milk is the imperishable eye in the *nṛyajña*; and curd is likewise in the *pitṛyajña*.
Together with the vajra. ||5||
One should establish the Lord Vāgvajrācārya, the supreme among all happiness and the king of kings,
who is pure, upon the ground of Varuṇa, Agni, Earth, Wind, and the Devas, within the Pure Land. ||5||
The five products of the cow and fine gold dust.
Blue, black, red, tawny, and white;
[these correspond] respectively to cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter. (6)
From these cows, one should take the five products for purification;
in their absence, however, one should especially take them from cows of all castes.
Salutations again and again to Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Saumyā, and Kapilā.
May Mahālakṣmī be gracious; may there be long life, health, and prosperity. (8)
Accompanied by this verse, one should again cause [the child] to eat food mixed with cow's products:
one pala of cow urine and half of that (half a pala) of cow dung.
One should take seven palas of milk, five palas of curd,
one pala of ghee, and likewise water from a sacred bathing place (tīrthodaka). ||10||
By this, the cow-product (gavya) has been prepared, which is like the thunderbolt of Indra;
the cow-product, consisting of the splendor of the mantra, is the destroyer of all sins. ||11||

By means of the mantra for entering the womb, evil goes to destruction. (28) One should cause the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) to be offered according to the distinctions of color and form. Thus [ends] the extraction from the *Sarvatathāgatadvādaśasāhasrapārājikāvinaya*.
The exposition of the names for liberation from sin, which issued forth from the lotus-like mouth of the glorious Lord of Sages, is complete.
May there be auspiciousness at all times! Thus, in the year [blank], in the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
